title: Finland's 24/7 Puppy Livestream Draws Millions
paragraphs: Six newborn puppies in Finland are winning over millions of viewers with every little wiggle and squeak.
The puppies are the stars of Pentulive, a 24/7 livestream from Finland's public broadcaster Yle. Pentu means "puppy" in Finnish.
The four males and two females were born on October 10 to a 5-year-old Lagotto Romagnolo named Hilkka. The brown-and-white puppies spend most of their time sleeping and nursing.
"They are just opening their eyes and their ears," Pirjo Koskinen, a Yle science journalist behind the idea for Pentulive, told The Associated Press. "They are taking their first clumsy steps."
The livestream is letting viewers follow the puppies as they grow. Yle also holds online chats three times a week, and has a podcast about how the pups are growing.
The show is now in its sixth season and is still very popular. In less than two weeks, the livestream received more than 6 million views on social media alone in Finland.
Watching the puppies is good for people, too.

Koskinen said watching them hurry to their mother for milk, for example, can increase levels of a hormone called oxytocin in the human brain. Also known as the "love hormone," it can help people feel closer to others and less anxious.

For many viewers, though, the show simply offers a break from all the stressful news we see every day. One look at those little tails and pink noses and it's hard not to smile, said Jyri Loikkanen from Yle.

Pentulive is an example of "slow TV", which focuses on long, quiet broadcasts of everyday events. This style of TV began in Norway in 2009 with a seven-hour train journey shown minute by minute and has since become popular in other countries.
